messages.subject: Re: unable to install protobuf
messages.body_plain:
Sandy,

protobuf-2.3.0.tar.gz  is not an R package. You can't install it using R CMD .

Typically one does

tar zxvf protobuf-2.3.0.tar.gz
cd protobuf*
./configure && make -j2 && sudo make install

(assuming you have root permissions and a dual core processor which makes things faster )

Cheers
Sapsi

messages.subject_clean: Just spent 3 hours looking for a bug
messages.body_plain:
I am filing this under what makes software hard to use; though I am
not advocating any adjustments.

I just spent 3 hours trying to find a bug in my code.  The reduce
key,values were not getting emitted after my pre,reduce,post.  Just a
silent 0 for Reduce output records.  Inspections of data in the post
with rhcounter revealed the emitted objects were present at the time
of rhcollect.  No error messages were otherwise present, and no job
failures were otherwise indicated.  The intended emission was the
reduce.key with a value that was  a matrix that was 12 million rows by
3 columns.  Emitting just a single row of the matrix worked, but
emitting the whole thing did not.

I spent 4 hours tweaking code, and finally while getting a soda I took
a guess about the problem that I think is right.

I think the value was over the byte limit that Rhipe accepts?  Will
that fail to emit silently in version 65.5)?

Silent failure made  me sad. Silent and deadly.

Code follows

ifolder = "/wsc/jrounds/marginal/convolution/simulation/
pooled.temporary"
ifolder = paste(ifolder,"/part-r-00001",sep="")
ofolder = "/wsc/jrounds/marginal/convolution/simulation/pooled"
inout = c("sequence","sequence")
mapred = list(  mapred.map.tasks = 9,
                mapred.reduce.tasks = 9,
                rhipe_map_buff_size=12,
                rhipe_reduce_buff_size=12)

idata = rhread(ifolder,"sequence",10)
keys = lapply(idata,function(d) d[[1]])
values = lapply(idata,function(d) d[[2]])
map = expression({
	for(i in seq_along(map.keys)){
        k = map.keys[[i]]
        v = map.values[[i]]

        rhcollect(k,v)

	}
})

reduce = expression(
    pre = {
        data = list()
    },
    reduce = {
        rhcounter("reduce","length values", length(reduce.values))
        data = append(data,reduce.values)
    },
    post = {
        d = do.call("rbind",data)
        rhcounter("reduce","nrow data", nrow(d))
        rhcollect(1,d)
    }

)

jobname = "Pool Convolution Simulation"
mr = rhmr(map = map, reduce=reduce,inout=inout,ifolder = ifolder,
ofolder=ofolder, jobname = jobname,mapred=mapred)
ex = rhex(mr, async=TRUE)

rhls(ofolder)
odata = rhread(ofolder, "sequence",1)

messages.subject: Re: [rhipe] RHMRMapper
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This is a good question and I'll try and elaborate on this.
Here in Mozilla, crash report data is stored as JSON objects in a
HBase table. The keys are salted for load balancing
but the values are JSON strings.

How to make RHIPE work with a HBase source. One has two options

a) Use RJava to :
  1) find how many RegionSplits and set N to that value, use
inout[1]=="lapply" and call the Hbase API via rJava to get access to
the objects. Note you can call rJava from within RHIPE.

b) With a bit of effort, write you own InputFormat in Java. This is
what i did here at Mozilla, created a small JAR file that had it's own
inputFormat, and some RHBytesWritable subclasses. The RHIPE code
looks like (sadly I lost the source! But i'll rewrite and place it on github)

hbasemap <- function(tablename, colspec,
rows,dateformat="yyyyMMdd",cacheBlocks=3L, caching=TRUE){
  mapred <- list()
  mapred$rhipe.hbase.tablename <- as.character(tablename[1])
  mapred$rhipe.hbase.colspec <- paste(colspec,collapse=",")
  mapred$rhipe.hbase.rowlim.start <-rows[1]
  mapred$rhipe.hbase.rowlim.end <- rows[2]
  mapred$rhipe.hbase.mozilla.dateformat <- "yyyyMMdd"
  mapred$rhipe.hbase.mozilla.cacheblocks <- sprintf("%s:%s",
as.integer(cacheBlocks), tolower(as.character(caching)))
  mapred$rhipe_inputformat_class <-
'com.mozilla.hadoop.hbase.rhipe.RHMultiScanTableInputFormat'
  mapred$rhipe_inputformat_keyclass <- 'com.mozilla.hadoop.hbase.rhipe.RHNull'
  mapred$rhipe_inputformat_valueclass <-
'com.mozilla.hadoop.hbase.rhipe.RHResult'
  mapred
}

map <- expression(
    lapply(map.values,function(r){
        rhcollect(NULL,r)
      })
    )

## Zero throttling was done from  03/22/2011 -   00:00
03/29/201103/22/2011 -   00:00 03/29/2011
## The JAR file (akela) contains the Inputformat to read hbase
(com.mozilla.hadoop.hbase.rhipe.RHMultiScanTableInputFormat)

mapred <- hbasemap("crash_reports" ,
colspec="meta_data:json,processed_data:json,timestamps:submitted"
,rows=c("20110322","20110328"))
mapred$mapred.reduce.tasks <- 0
z <- rhmr(rmap=rcode  ,ofolder='/user/sguha/tmp/zerothrottle'
,inout=c(NA,'seq')   ,zips="/user/sguha/Rfolder.tar.gz"
,jarfiles="/user/sguha/tmp/akela-0.1.jar",
          ,jobname='Rhipe and Hbase?'  ,mapred=mapred)

rhstatus(rhex(z,async=TRUE),mon.sec=5)

messages.subject: Re: [rhipe] What is the difference between RHIPE,HIVE,Hadoop Streaming R packages to R on hadoop
messages.subject_clean: [rhipe] What is the difference between RHIPE,HIVE,Hadoop Streaming R packages to R on hadoop
messages.body_plain:
Sandeep - Of those 3 options you tested a short answer it to use RHIPE, since it provides various advantages over straight streaming, including performance based on my (admittedly limited) testing. A better answer requires evaluating the specific applications you're looking to implement, as well as things like your environment, etc (e.g. physical cluster vs. cloud). The presentation that accompanies the example code on github is here: http://www.slideshare.net/jseidman/distributed-data-analysis-with-r-strangeloop-2011

If you look at the end of the deck you'll note that we provide our recommendations for which tool to use when, so this might help out a little. messages.subject: Re: What is the difference between RHIPE,HIVE,Hadoop Streaming R packages to R on hadoop
messages.subject_clean: What is the difference between RHIPE,HIVE,Hadoop Streaming R packages to R on hadoop
messages.body_plain:
You can basically accomplish everything with streaming if performance
and file size wasn't an issue. and it is a useful way to go if you
just want to dabble in R Hadoop interactions to get the idea,  but
Saptarshi built a number of performance improvements into Rhipe over
Streaming and also he has made some things more convenient. Once Rhipe
is setup it is simpler to use then doing everything by hand with
streaming.  It is sort of an educational and useful exercise to do
something with streaming once.  Works better with simulations that are
inherently small data problems but problems such that you can  benefit
with throwing a lot of cores at them.  For example, some bayesian
posterior simulations.  The optimizations Rhipe provides are better
suited toward truly large data problems where you are really going to
notice them.

> Streaming and also he has made some things more convenient. Once Rhipe
